positions/annihilationism/oneLine: Immortality is God’s gift in Christ, not an innate property of the soul; the unrepentant, after judgement and a just measure of punishment, finally perish and cease to exist.
positions/annihilationism/coreClaims/0: Only God has immortality (1 Tim 6:16); eternal life is given to those in Christ.
positions/annihilationism/coreClaims/1: Biblical language of death, destruction, perishing and consuming fire means the end of existence.
positions/annihilationism/coreClaims/2: The punishment is "eternal" in its result (irreversible destruction), not in conscious duration.
positions/annihilationism/coreClaims/3: The doctrine of the immortal soul owes more to Plato than to Scripture.
positions/annihilationism/origin: Precursors in Arnobius (c.300) and some Socinians; revived by 19th-century writers (Edward White, Life in Christ, 1846) and Adventists; brought into evangelical mainstream by Basil Atkinson, Edward Fudge (The Fire That Consumes, 1982) and John Stott (1988).
positions/annihilationism/strongestArgum: It takes biblical destruction language literally and avoids importing Greek immortality.
It removes the moral objection to unending torment while maintaining real judgement.
It fits texts where God finally makes all things new without an eternal realm of evil.
positions/annihilationism/strongestObjec: Matthew 25:46 parallels eternal punishment with eternal life, and Revelation 14:11 and 20:10 speak of torment "for ever and ever".
It breaks with the dominant Christian tradition since Augustine.
Critics argue it lessens the gravity of sin against an infinite God.
positions/annihilationism/responses/0: Conditionalists reply that "eternal punishment" can mean an irreversible punishment ("eternal judgement", Heb 6:2) and that Revelation’s imagery is symbolic.
positions/annihilationism/responses/1: They point out that the 2000 Evangelical Alliance (UK) report treated it as a legitimate evangelical view.
positions/annihilationism/consequences/0: Official teaching of Seventh-day Adventists and Jehovah’s Witnesses (the latter outside Nicene orthodoxy).
positions/annihilationism/consequences/1: A widely tolerated minority view among evangelicals since the 1980s.
positions/eternal-conscious-punishment/o: Those who die unreconciled to God will experience unending, conscious separation and punishment, as the just consequence of sin against an infinitely holy God.
positions/eternal-conscious-punishment/c: Jesus speaks of "eternal punishment" parallel to "eternal life" (Matt 25:46).
The soul (and resurrected body) is created to exist without end.
Punishment is just retribution, not merely corrective.
The final state is fixed at death or judgement; there is no post-mortem conversion.
positions/eternal-conscious-punishment/o: Majority view of the patristic church from Tertullian and Augustine (City of God XXI, c.426); confirmed against Origenism (543/553), in the Athanasian Creed and Fourth Lateran (1215), and in the Reformation confessions (e.g. Westminster 33.2).
positions/eternal-conscious-punishment/s: It is the most straightforward reading of Jesus’ own words and of Revelation.
It represents the near-unanimous judgement of the church through most of its history.
It upholds the seriousness of sin, human freedom and the urgency of evangelism.
Moral objection: infinite punishment for finite sins seems disproportionate and incompatible with divine love.
Conditionalists: it assumes Greek immortality of the soul.
Universalists: an eternal realm of evil means God is never "all in all".
positions/eternal-conscious-punishment/r: Traditionalists answer that sin against an infinite God is infinitely serious and that the damned continue in rebellion.
Many modern defenders (C. S. Lewis) stress hell as self-chosen: "the doors of hell are locked on the inside".
positions/eternal-conscious-punishment/c: Shaped preaching, art (Dante, Michelangelo) and revivalism for centuries.
Remains the official teaching of most churches.
positions/sola-scriptura/oneLine: Holy Scripture is the only infallible rule of faith and practice; creeds, councils and church teachers are real but subordinate authorities to be tested by it.
positions/sola-scriptura/coreClaims/0: Scripture is the inspired Word of God and the supreme norm (norma normans) for doctrine.
positions/sola-scriptura/coreClaims/1: Scripture is sufficient: all things necessary for salvation are set down in it or deduced from it (Westminster Confession 1.6; Thirty-Nine Articles 6).
positions/sola-scriptura/coreClaims/2: Scripture is clear (perspicuous) in what is necessary for salvation and interprets itself (Scriptura sui ipsius interpres).
positions/sola-scriptura/coreClaims/3: Popes and councils can err and have erred; their decrees bind only insofar as they agree with Scripture.
positions/sola-scriptura/coreClaims/4: Scripture's authority is recognised through the inner witness of the Holy Spirit, not conferred by the church (Calvin).
positions/sola-scriptura/origin: Anticipated by Wycliffe and Hus; formulated by Martin Luther in his conflict with Rome (Leipzig Disputation 1519, Diet of Worms 1521); confessionally defined in the Formula of Concord (1577), the Thirty-Nine Articles (1563/1571), the Belgic Confession (1561) and the Westminster Confession (1647).
positions/sola-scriptura/proponentsOther: Martin Chemnitz (Examination of the Council of Trent)
Keith Mathison (modern, distinguishing it from ‘solo scriptura’)
positions/sola-scriptura/strongestArgume: Only Scripture is ‘God-breathed’ (2 Timothy 3:16); all other authorities are human and fallible.
Jesus judged the traditions of the elders by the written Word (Mark 7).
Church history shows that popes and councils have contradicted one another (e.g. Honorius condemned by a council, conflicting papal claims during the Western Schism).
It makes possible reform of the church and gives every believer direct access to God's Word in the vernacular.
positions/sola-scriptura/strongestObject: Scripture nowhere teaches that Scripture alone is the rule of faith; 2 Thessalonians 2:15 commends oral tradition.
The canon itself was recognised by the church's tradition, which sola scriptura cannot account for without circularity.
Protestantism has fragmented into many denominations disagreeing on interpretation, suggesting Scripture alone is not sufficiently clear.
In practice Protestants also rely on traditions (creeds, confessions, interpretive communities).
positions/sola-scriptura/responses/0: Reformers distinguished sola scriptura from ‘solo scriptura’ (‘nuda scriptura’): tradition and creeds are valued as ministerial, not magisterial, authorities.
positions/sola-scriptura/responses/1: The church recognises the canon as a shepherd recognises a flock's voice — it does not create it (John 10:27).
positions/sola-scriptura/responses/2: Disagreements exist equally within Catholicism and Orthodoxy; Scripture is clear on the essentials of salvation.
positions/sola-scriptura/responses/3: The apostolic oral tradition of 2 Thessalonians was inscripturated; no other verifiable apostolic deposit remains.
positions/sola-scriptura/consequences/0: Vernacular Bible translation, literacy and preaching-centred worship across Protestant cultures.
positions/sola-scriptura/consequences/1: Multiplication of confessions and denominations; a tension between individual interpretation and confessional authority.
positions/sola-scriptura/consequences/2: Foundation for later evangelical, Pentecostal and global-South Bible movements and Bible societies (British and Foreign Bible Society, 1804).
positions/scripture-and-tradition/name: Scripture and Tradition under the Magisterium (Catholic)
positions/scripture-and-tradition/oneLin: God's revelation is handed on in Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition, which form one sacred deposit of the Word of God, authentically interpreted by the living teaching office (Magisterium) of the bishops in communion with the pope.
positions/scripture-and-tradition/coreCl: Christ entrusted the gospel to the apostles, who handed it on in preaching, example, institutions and writings.
Scripture and Tradition flow from the same divine wellspring and are to be accepted with equal devotion and reverence (Trent; Dei Verbum 9).
The Magisterium is not above the Word of God but serves it, teaching only what has been handed on (Dei Verbum 10).
The Church recognised and defined the canon, including the deuterocanonical books.
Doctrine develops organically over time (Newman) without changing in substance.
positions/scripture-and-tradition/origin: Rooted in Irenaeus, Tertullian (Prescription against Heretics), Basil and Vincent of Lérins; defined against the Reformers at Trent, Session IV (1546); refined at Vatican I (Dei Filius, 1870) and Vatican II (Dei Verbum, 1965).
positions/scripture-and-tradition/strong: Historically, the church existed and taught before the New Testament was written or collected; the canon was recognised by the church's tradition.
Scripture itself commends unwritten tradition and points to the church as ‘the pillar and ground of the truth’ (1 Timothy 3:15).
A living, authoritative interpreter is needed to resolve disputes, as at the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15).
It provides doctrinal unity across a global communion of over a billion members.
Protestants argue that it subordinates Scripture to the church in practice, allowing doctrines with little biblical basis (e.g. Marian dogmas).
Tradition is too broad and inconsistent to function as a reliable norm; the Fathers disagree among themselves.
Orthodox critics argue the Magisterium, especially the papacy, has displaced the conciliar mind of the whole church.
Historical criticism shows that some ‘traditions’ claimed as apostolic arose later.
positions/scripture-and-tradition/respon: Catholics answer that every interpretive community has a tradition; the question is whether it is accountable and apostolic.
Newman's theory of development explains how later doctrines unfold what was implicit in revelation.
Vatican II explicitly subordinated the Magisterium to the Word of God and encouraged biblical study and vernacular Scripture.
positions/scripture-and-tradition/conseq: Trent's decree fixed the Catholic canon and the authority of the Vulgate until the 20th century.
Enabled definitions such as the Immaculate Conception (1854) and Assumption (1950).
Vatican II's Dei Verbum opened Catholic biblical scholarship and ecumenical dialogue on Scripture and Tradition.
positions/holy-tradition-orthodox/name: Scripture within Holy Tradition (Eastern and Oriental Orthodox)
positions/holy-tradition-orthodox/oneLin: Holy Scripture is the supreme expression of Holy Tradition — the life of the Holy Spirit in the Church — interpreted through the Fathers, the ecumenical councils, the liturgy and icons, and guarded by the whole people of God rather than by any single office.
positions/holy-tradition-orthodox/coreCl: Tradition is not a second source beside Scripture but the living memory of the Church in which Scripture is read.
The ecumenical councils, received by the whole Church, are infallible expressions of its faith.
The liturgy is a primary interpreter of Scripture (lex orandi, lex credendi).
No single bishop, including the bishop of Rome, has infallibility apart from the Church.
The Septuagint is the authoritative Old Testament text.
positions/holy-tradition-orthodox/origin: Expressed by Basil (On the Holy Spirit 27), Vincent of Lérins, John of Damascus and the Seventh Ecumenical Council (787); formulated against Protestant and Catholic positions by the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) and the Encyclical of the Eastern Patriarchs (1848); developed by Khomiakov (sobornost), Florovsky (‘neo-patristic synthesis’) and Ware.
positions/holy-tradition-orthodox/strong: It reflects how Scripture was actually received: within worshipping communities guided by bishops and councils.
It avoids both Protestant individualism and the concentration of authority in one office.
Continuity of liturgy and doctrine across many cultures and centuries under pressure (Arab, Ottoman, Soviet) without a central magisterium.
Protestants: it places tradition beyond biblical correction, allowing practices such as icon veneration to be made binding.
Catholics: without a final arbiter, the Orthodox cannot convene ecumenical councils or settle disputes (e.g. disputes between patriarchates, 2018 Moscow–Constantinople schism).
The criterion of ‘reception’ seems circular: a council is ecumenical if received, and received if orthodox.
positions/holy-tradition-orthodox/respon: Orthodox theologians answer that the Holy Spirit, not a juridical office, guarantees truth, and reception is the Spirit's work in the Church.
Scripture holds primacy within Tradition, and the Fathers are honoured precisely as interpreters of Scripture.
positions/holy-tradition-orthodox/conseq: Underpins the Orthodox rejection of papal infallibility and the Filioque.
Explains the authority of icons, liturgy and the canons in Orthodox life.
Shapes Orthodox participation in ecumenism, especially the World Council of Churches.
